newsitem.title: USA: Random House skips book show, but executives attend.
newsitem.headline: Random House skips book show, but executives attend.

text.p: Top executives of book publishing giant Random House were spotted here at BookExpo America, although their firm was one of several big publishers officially absent from the industry convention.
Random House Chairman Alberto Vitale and top manager Philip Pfeffer attended an American Booksellers Association briefing Sunday on its annual consumer book-buying study.
"It's a good sign for the convention that they came," said Sandra Paul, who manages the association's Book Industry Study Group.
The appearance of Vitale and Pfeffer may indicate some rapprochement between book publishers and booksellers, whose disputes hurt the show this year.

BookExpo opened this weekend with the usual autograph sessions, lavish authors' parties and hordes of freebie gatherers, but total floor space covered at the cavernous McCormick Center was down by about a quarter from last year and regulars said attendance was off. The organizers of the show, which ends Monday, did not release attendance figures.

Celebrating its 50th anniversary, the convention this year suffered from the withdrawal of Random House, Simon & Schuster, Bantam Doubleday Dell and several mid-sized publishers. They abandoned the show after fighting in court for two years with booksellers who had accused them of unfair pricing policies.
The legal disputes are largely over, and the booksellers have sold the show to a unit of Reed Elsevier, an Anglo-Dutch media firm, but tension remains.

Some major publishers, such as Warner Books, showed up as usual this year with large displays of new and upcoming titles. Besides Random House, other big companies were rumored to have unofficial delegations either at the show or working on its periphery in Chicago hotel rooms.

Bookstore owners and buyers, to whom the publishers normally pitch their wares during the show, said the feel of it had changed. "I miss the big publishers because they had everything," said Susan Heimann, a buyer of computer books for Page One Bookstore in Albuquerque, N.M.

But she added that a smaller, less-cluttered show has allowed smaller publishers to get more attention and freed up space for commerce. "Before you were always getting jostled by someone trying to grab a free pen or something. At this one, I'll tell you, a lot more business is getting done," she said.
Would she come again next year if the major houses refused to return?
"I don't know," she said. "It's a major expense and things are lean."
